ai.literal: Having thought, one thing will you not say, O heart, even in any small measure, the medicine that cures this painful affliction?
ai.translation: O my heart! Can you not think of and tell me some remedy, even a tiny one, that will cure this painful affliction of love?
ai.modern: நெஞ்சே! இந்தத் துன்பத் துயரத்தைத் தீர்க்கும் ஏதேனும் ஒரு மருந்தை (வழியை) யோசித்து எனக்குச் சொல்ல மாட்டாயா?
ai.explanation: The heroine, suffering deeply from the pain of separation, addresses her own heart as a companion. She asks it to think deeply and suggest at least one remedy (ஒன்று சொல்லாயோ) to cure her suffering. She refers to her love-sickness as 'evvanōy' (எவ்வநோய்), meaning a painful disease of distress. She pleads for any medicine (மருந்து), even the smallest possible cure (எனைத்தொன்றும்), showing her utter helplessness and desperation.

ai.literal: Love he does not have, since it is so, you suffering is foolishness; may you live, my heart!
ai.translation: Since he has no love for us, your grieving for him is sheer foolishness, my heart! May you live long.
ai.modern: அவர் நம்மிடம் அன்பு இல்லாதவராக இருக்க, என் நெஞ்சமே! நீ அவருக்காக வருந்துவது அறியாமையாகும்; நீ வாழ்க!
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine speaks to her own heart, which is deeply pining for her absent lover. She reasons that since he has shown no love by staying away, it is foolish for her heart to continue to suffer and ache for him. The phrase 'வாழி என் நெஞ்சு' (may you live, my heart) is a gentle, slightly ironic blessing used to address her own mind while pointing out its irrational behavior. The word 'பேதைமை' highlights the lack of wisdom in loving someone who does not return that love with equal intensity.

ai.literal: Staying here and thinking of him, what is the use of grieving, O heart? Lovingly thinking of us does not exist with the one who caused this distressing pain.
ai.translation: O my heart, what is the use of staying here, thinking of him and grieving? Any loving thought for us does not exist in the one who caused this distressing affliction.
ai.modern: நெஞ்சே! இங்கேயே இருந்து அவரை நினைத்து வருந்துவதால் என்ன பயன்? நமக்கு இந்தத் துன்ப நோயைத் தந்தவரிடத்தில் நம்மைப் பற்றி அன்போடு நினைக்கும் குணம் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: The heroine addresses her own heart, which is constantly dwelling on the memory of her departed lover and suffering from the pain of separation. She asks her heart what the point is of staying in one place, thinking of him, and grieving. She points out that the lover, who caused this distressing affliction of love-sickness by leaving her, does not possess any loving or compassionate thoughts ('parintu uḷḷal') toward her. The contrast between her heart's constant yearning ('uḷḷi parital') and the lover's lack of reciprocal concern highlights the painful asymmetry of her grief.

The metaphor of the eyes 'eating' her vividly portrays the painful, gnawing sensation of unfulfilled desire.

words.gloss: those who do not love us

ai.literal: O heart! Saying that they disliked us, is there abandoning them, when they are those who do not love us even if we love them?
ai.translation: O my heart! Is it possible for us to abandon him saying 'he dislikes us', when he is one who does not love us even when we love him?
ai.modern: நெஞ்சே! நாம் அன்பு செய்தாலும் நம்மிடம் அன்பு செய்யாதவராகிய அவரை, 'அவர் நம்மை வெறுத்துவிட்டார்' என்று கூறி நம்மால் கைவிட முடியுமா?
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine speaks to her own heart about her inability to let go of her lover. She asks her heart if they can truly abandon him under the excuse that he dislikes or is angry with them (செற்றார்). She points out the bitter truth: he is already someone who does not return their love (உறாஅதவர்) even when they love him deeply (யாம் உற்றால்). Since they could not stop loving him despite his indifference, they cannot easily cast him aside now just because of his apparent hostility.

ai.literal: Having mingled and appeasing lover if you see, having sulked you do not realize; false anger you show, my heart!
ai.translation: O my heart! If you see our lover who comes to embrace and appease us, you forget to remain sulky; yet, in his absence, you show only a false anger.
ai.modern: கூடி அணைத்துத் தன் அன்பைப் புரியவைக்கும் காதலரைக் கண்டால், நீ ஊடல் கொள்வதை மறந்துவிடுகிறாய்; என் நெஞ்சமே! இப்போது மட்டும் அவரிடம் வீணாகப் பொய்க் கோபம் கொள்கிறாய்.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine speaks to her own heart, pointing out its inconsistency. She notes that when her lover is present, ready to embrace and comfort her, her heart completely forgets its resolve to remain sulky ('pulantu uṇarāy'). However, in his absence, the heart pretends to be angry and vows to show resentment. Thus, she chides her heart for harboring a 'false anger' ('poykkāyvu') that vanishes the moment the lover appears.

ai.literal: Love let go of either one, or modesty let go, O good heart! As for me, I cannot bear these two.
ai.translation: O my good heart, either give up desire or give up modesty; as for me, I cannot endure both at the same time.
ai.modern: நல்ல நெஞ்சே! காமத்தை விட்டுவிடு அல்லது நாணத்தை விட்டுவிடு. என்னால் இந்த இரண்டையும் ஒன்றாகத் தாங்கிக்கொள்ள முடியாது.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine addresses her own heart, which is caught in a painful conflict. She is torn between her intense love (kāmam) and her sense of modesty (nāṇ), which prevents her from seeking her lover. She tells her heart to choose one and abandon the other, as she cannot bear the burden of holding onto both opposing feelings simultaneously. The word 'poṟēn' highlights her inability to endure this internal struggle any longer.

ai.literal: He who once showed love will not bestow grace, thinking thus and yearning, behind him who departed you go, foolish my heart!
ai.translation: O my foolish heart! Yearning and thinking, 'He who once showed love will no longer bestow his grace,' you still go running after him who departed.
ai.modern: முன்பு அன்பு காட்டியவர் இப்போது அருள் செய்யமாட்டார் என்று ஏங்கி வருந்தியும், நம்மை விட்டுப் பிரிந்து சென்றவரின் பின்னே போகிறாய்; என் நெஞ்சமே, நீ மிகவும் பேதை!
ai.explanation: The heroine addresses her own heart, which is longing to go after her departed lover. She calls her heart foolish ('பேதை') because it is caught in a painful contradiction. On one hand, the heart laments and realizes that the lover, who once showed great affection ('பரிந்தவர்'), has now departed and will not return to bestow his grace ('நல்கார்'). On the other hand, despite knowing this painful truth, the heart still desperately wants to follow him ('பின்செல்வாய்'). This internal dialogue highlights the helplessness of love, where the mind's rational understanding of abandonment is overpowered by the heart's uncontrollable yearning.

words.gloss: he who resides within the mind

ai.literal: He who is in the mind, as the beloved, thinking of him, you, to whom, do you go, my heart?
ai.translation: O my heart! Since my beloved resides constantly within you, whom are you going in search of, and where?
ai.modern: என் நெஞ்சே! காதலரானவர் உனக்குள்ளேயே இருக்க, அவரை நினைத்துக்கொண்டு நீ யாரிடம் போகிறாய்?
ai.explanation: The heroine addresses her own heart, which is longing to go to her distant lover. She points out the irony that the lover already dwells constantly within her mind (உள்ளத்தார்). Since he is already inside, there is no need for the heart to travel anywhere else to seek him. By asking 'to whom do you go?' (யாருழைச் சேறி), she highlights that any outward journey of the mind is redundant when the beloved is already fully present within.

ai.literal: Without approaching us him who abandoned us, in our heart if we keep, still we will lose our beauty.
ai.translation: If we continue to keep him in our heart, who abandoned us without any desire to return, we will only go on losing our beauty.

ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine addresses her own heart, questioning its stubborn attachment to the departed lover. The word 'tunnā' describes the lover as someone who has abandoned her without any intention of approaching or showing affection. She warns her heart that by harboring him inside ('neñcattu uṭaiyēmā'), they are only prolonging their own grief. This internal sorrow manifests physically, causing her to continuously lose her natural beauty and luster ('kaviṉ').
